description_full: Noah Holdings Limited, together with its subsidiaries, operates as a wealth and asset management service provider with the focus on investment and asset allocation services for high net worth individuals and corporate entities in Mainland of China, Hong Kong, and internationally. It operates through Domestic Public Securities, Domestic Asset Management, Domestic Insurance, Overseas Wealth Management, Overseas Asset Management, and Overseas Insurance and Comprehensive Services segments. The company offers mutual fund products, which are publicly-raised, public securities investment funds, including money market funds; private secondary products; private equity products; investor education; trust services; and insurance products by referring clients, as well as individual whole life insurance, participating insurance, and individual health insurance products. It also provides domestic and overseas private equity, FOFs, public securities, real estate, and multi-strategy and other investments, as well as manages feeder funds. Noah Holdings Limited was founded in 2005 and is headquartered in Singapore.
ceo_bio: Mr. Zhe  Yin | Co-Founder, CEO & Director | Age 51 | Compensation: $532,479 (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 1K people. Revenue per employee of $250K ranks in the bottom quartile among Financial Services peers, with revenue growing 7%/yr across its filed history. Each employee generates $80K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $6K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 2× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity).
financial_summary: Noah Holdings Limited is a small-cap financial services business with a $448M market cap on $395M of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at -8% over the past three years and +7% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome. Operating margins are contracting by -2.1pp, the first warning that competitive pressure is eroding the franchise.
Returns on capital run at 18% against a 11% cost of capital, a 8-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it.

The business throws off $126M in free cash flow — roughly 32 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.75× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year.

Management returns a meaningful 20.1% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: Its 30% operating margin is roughly in line with the Financial Services median (29%).
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.14x).
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-19.5% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.02 across 514 companies in the universe; the top four hold 20% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a steep downtrend, down 22% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 48% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 29% and a beta of 1.21, it amplifies market moves, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.47 vs 5y 1.36), so read it loosely.
Trading is thin (about $945K a day), below the $1.0M liquidity floor flagged; building a position would move the price.
In past sell-offs it fell 47% in the 2020 crash and 63% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The stock trades 82% below its DCF fair value of $35.58, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 37%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $30.87 to $42.00 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Financial Services peers: P/E 5.4 vs 12.3 and P/FCF 3.5 vs 13.0 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 52% below its 10-year median.
The 4 covering analysts target $10.29 on average, 58% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 18% clears the cost of capital of 10.5% by 8pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 2.50).
It converts 32% of revenue into free cash flow.
It earns a 6% return on equity.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -7.7% over 3 years, -5.4% over 5 years and 7.5% over 10 years, so the decline is deepening, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 49%).
At current returns, reinvesting 15% of profits supports about 2.7% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
Analysts expect 1.1% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.6%), and institutions hold 38%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (14 sales, net $126K sold).
It returns 20.1% a year to shareholders (1.8% in buybacks and 10.0% in dividends).
The share count has grown 64.1% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
people: With about 1,582 employees, each generates about $250K of revenue, 0.5x the Financial Services median, and revenue has grown 7.5% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $80K of free cash flow per employee.
The company is founder-led, which often keeps management aligned with long-term owners.
